# Setup and Pre-Processing

## Working Directory

Before we start find the working directory (a folder in which RStudio stores its output)

You can also set a new working directory with the setwd() function if you are not happy with the selected working directory. Just copy the path to a folder you like into the brackets in quotation marks and change all \ to /.

Example: setwd("C:/User/.../CTA")

```{r}
getwd()


```

## Installing Packages

Next you install the packages you might need and load those you use (through the library function).

```{r}
packages <- c("tidyverse","quanteda","quanteda.textstats",
"quanteda.textplots","quanteda.textmodels","readtext","rmarkdown","knitr")
install.packages(setdiff(packages, rownames(installed.packages())),
                 repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")

library(tidyverse)
library(quanteda)
library(quanteda.textmodels)
library(quanteda.textplots)
library(quanteda.textstats)
library(readtext)

```

## Working with text: Creating objects, creating a corpus 

Now we are ready to create objects to work with. Get the "eurydice" file from my website. Copy the path to the RDS document "eurydice" and use the readRDS() function to import it into the environment. Create a new object for the corpus that only includes the features of the RDS imported. Use the corpus() function.

Other data formats can be imported with different commands such as readtext() or read.csv()

```{r}
eurydice <- readRDS("C:/Users...eurydice.RDS")

```


## Creating a corpus

Before we can work with the text we need to define it as corpus using the corpus() function. Select a name of your choice for the corpus, e.g. corpus_eurydice.

```{r}
name <- corpus(eurydice)

```


## Tokenization

At word, sentence or character level. We will tokenize at word level and store tokenized text in new object. Type a name for an object (e.g. "eurydice_toks <-") before the function (tokens). Then add the name of your corpus,  which you assigned above (e.g. corpus_eurydice).

If you want, try out how tokenization as sentence or character level affects the representation of the text. 

```{r}
eurydice_toks_word <- tokens(name,"word")
eurydice_toks_sentence <- tokens(name ,"sentence")
eurydice_toks_character <- tokens(name,"character")
systems_toks <- tokens(name)


```

## Document-Feature-Matrix

Create a document-feature-matrix. Store it in the environment by assigning a name (e.g. dfm_eurydice <- dfm(systems_toks)). Look at the dfm by typing its name in again without any function attached (e.g.dfm_eurydice).

```{r}


```

# Pre-processing

Let's start pre-processing to remove features that are not text (1), to remove uninformative features (2), and to unite features that should be understood as one (3).


## Let's first understand the dfm we have created through some quick operations

1. Number of tokens per document. replace x with name of dfm.
```{r}
ntoken(x) %>% head()

```

2. The number of features in our dfm. use the function nfeat()
```{r}


```

3. The top features before pre-processing (run this again after pre-processing). You know the function already.
```{r}


```

4. The number of documents in our dfm. Use the ndoc() function.
```{r}


```

5. The frequency of features. Replace x with the name of your dfm. The code shows how often each feature occurs in the whole dfm, summed over all documents. head() only shows the first six features, which are not sorted by frequency, so this is just a quick look at how the output is structured. To see the most frequent features, you can sort the result with sort(featfreq(x), decreasing = TRUE) %>% head().

```{r}
featfreq(x) %>% head()

```

### Pre-processing step 1: Removing non-text
Replace x with the correct names of the different objects you refer too. Before "<-" always a new name for the object you are now storing (e.g. dfm_eurydice_clean). Never use the same name you already use for something else. In bracket always the name of what object to function should use. In the first line of code you need the dfm (e.g. dfm_eurydice) since you want to know the number of features in the dfm before cleaning. In the second line of code you first assign a new name for the cleaned tokenised corpus (e.g. toks_eurydice_clean). The x in the bracket here refers to the corpus (e.g. corpus_eurydice). The next line of code requires a new name for the cleaned dfm (e.g. dfm_eurydice_clean). The x in the dfm function refers to the tokenised object created in the last line (e.g.toks_eurydice_clean). The last line of code here requires the name of the new dfm (e.g. dfm_eurydice_clean)

```{r}
# To compare swiftly: How many features do we have before removing non-text?
nfeat(x)

# Now we remove punctuation, numbers and symbols
x <- tokens(x,  remove_punct=T,
  remove_numbers=T, remove_symbols=T)
x <- dfm(x)

# How many features does our dfm hold now? Much less!
nfeat(x)

```

### Pre-processing step 2: Removing uninformative text
```{r}
# Texts often contain words that are confounding the analysis. They are also called stopwords. See a list of English language stopwords here:

stopwords("en")

#Let's remove them.Same procedure as before, but we can remove in the dfm. Simply assign a new name and then replace x in bracket with name of the dfm. Then compare the number of features after cleaning and before cleaning. How many were removed?

x <- dfm_remove(x,stopwords("en")) 
nfeat(x)


#We can also remove the stopwords in other languages. Do this for German (stopwords("de"))


```

We can also trim the dfm to exclude words that appear too rarely to matter or too often to be informative (for example the name of the author of the document might appear on every page). Trimming can be based on how often a feature occurs in total across all documents (termfreq) and in how many documents it occurs (docfreq).

We will remove features that occur less than 50 times in total (min_termfreq), that occur in fewer than 5 documents (min_docfreq) or that occur more than 999 times in total (max_termfreq). The verbose option shows how many features were removed. Replace the first x with a new name for the trimmed dfm (e.g. dfm_eurydice_trimmed) and the second x with the name of your cleaned dfm. Leave the numbers as they are for now. Nothing needs to be added in the brackets of nfeat(). How many features are removed? Is this a wise pre-processing step?

```{r}
x <- dfm_trim(x, min_termfreq = 50,
              min_docfreq = 5,
              max_termfreq = 999, verbose = TRUE)

nfeat(x)

```

Which features would you remove? Decide yourself what to keep and what to remove. First create the untrimmed dfm from the toks object, then remove stopwords again and then run the dfm_trim function according to what you think helps.
```{r}


```

### Pre-processing step 3: Uniting features that share a common meaning

If we reduce the features to their wordstem, we unite words with the same meaning. E.g. "systems" and "system" or "programm" and "programme".Use the function dfm_wordstem(x, "en"). Find out how many features are left.
```{r}


```

### Adding docvars to the dfm

Add the variables "country" and "chapter" from the original data set to the dfm you have saved in the environment. This will be useful to compare between different groups. Replace the first x with the dfm you want to work with and the "eurydice" with the name you gave the originally important dataset or the corpus.

```{r}

docvars(x, "country") <- eurydice$country
docvars(x, "chapter") <- eurydice$chapter



```


### Advanced Transformations

If you want to learn how to  manipulate text data these operations will be useful for you:

1. Create a subset of your data set based on docvars (country, year,...). You choose which cases will be dropped: dfm_subset(dfm,docvar!="value") or kept dfm_subset(dfm,docvar=="value"). Replace dfm with a real dfm name (e.g. dfm_eurydice_clean), "docvar" with a document variable like country or chapter and the x with the value you are interested in (e.g. "France").

2. You can group documents based on docvars. Grouping combines all documents that share the same value of a document variable (e.g. country or year) and adds up their word counts. This lets you compare groups instead of single texts, for example the most frequent words per country or how language changes over year. 
Code: dfm_grouped <- dfm_group(dfm, groups = docvar)

Replace `dfm` with a real dfm name (e.g. `dfm_eurydice_clean`) and `docvar` with a document variable (e.g. `country`). 

Afterwards you can, for example, look at the top features of each group with `topfeatures(dfm_grouped, groups = docvar)`

# Descriptive Analysis

Let's get started on the analysis of text. First we will look at the absolute frequency of words through topfeatures and wordclouds, then at the relative word frequency through keywords (= words that are very frequent in one group of texts compared to the overall corpus).

## Topfeatures: Absolute frequency

How have the topfeatures changed after pre-processing? What can we learn here? Use the topfeatures() function two times: Once on the dfm before pre-processing/cleaning and once on the dfm after cleaning.
```{r}


```

## Wordclouds: Absolute frequency

You can visualize your finding through a wordcloud. You can choose the amount of words visible.You can also subset the dfm to analyse specific groups of texts. How do Germany and the overall corpus differ? Use the textplot_wordcloud(x, max_words = x) function for the overall dfm as well as a subset only consisting of the texts on one country, e.g. France or Germany.

```{r}


```


## Keywords: Relative frequency

Let's look at the relative word frequency through keywords (= words that are very frequent in one group of texts compared to the overall corpus). You will have to select a group you compare to the overall corpus. Try this out for different countries. Try to interpret the results.
Use the code below but change two things:

1. In `dfm_group()`, replace `dfm` with the name of your dfm (e.g. `dfm_eurydice_clean`). Leave `country` as it is. It is the document variable by which the documents are grouped, so the code creates one document per country.

2. In `textstat_keyness()`, replace `"x"` with the country you want to examine, in quotation marks (e.g."Germany" or "France"). The name must be spelled exactly as in your data.

Nothing needs to be added in the brackets of `head()` and `textplot_keyness()`. The pipe `%>%` passes the result of the previous line into the next function, so these functions get their input automatically.

Interpreting the plot: words on the right side of the plot are over-represented in the selected country (the target), words on the left are over-represented in all other countries combined. Try out different countries and ask yourself which words surprise you and why

```{r}
keyness <- dfm_group(dfm,country) %>%
 textstat_keyness("x")

head(keyness)

keyness %>%
 textplot_keyness()


```


## Bonus: Readability

For the analysis of some texts it is helpful to analyse the quality of text. There are different measures to do it. One way to do it is to find readability scores. Use the "textstat_readability()" function. Only look at the readability of some documents using the head function.

For this analysis, use the corpus and not the dfm. Readability scores are calculated from whole sentences and words in the running text (for example sentence length and word length), and a dfm has lost this information because it only contains word counts (the bag of words). Replace `corpus_eurydice` with the name of your corpus. The readability object goes into the brackets of `head()`.

What you will find: a table with one row per document and a readability score for each. The Flesch score is higher for easier texts (roughly 0 to 100; texts below 30 are very difficult, above 60 are easy to read). Very low or odd values can point to problems in the data, such as very short texts, tables, lists, so the scores are also a quick way to check the quality of your texts.

```{r}

readability <- textstat_readability(corpus_eurydice)

head(readability)

```
